newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Olympics-Sydney Games organisers attack ad ambushers.
newsitem.headline: Olympics-Sydney Games organisers attack ad ambushers.

text.p: The battle over Olympic marketing took a new twist on Thursday when organisers of the Sydney 2000 Games (SOCOG) announced an advertising campaign to stem the threat of "ambush marketing".

SOCOG media manager Richard Palfreyman said International Olympic Committee (IOC) officials were concerned about the increasing trend and had given the all-clear for SOCOG to launch a counter-offensive.
Ambush marketing is the term given to promotional campaigns run alongside an event by companies that do not hold rights to that event.

Palfreyman said the most publicised example was at last year's Atlanta Games when U.S. sportswear company Nike, a non-sponsor, arranged promotions and massive signpost advertising near Olympic stadiums.
"The IOC is very keen to see their sponsors protected," Palfreyman said.
"We wouldn't be able to stage the Games without them and it's important that they are protected."
The situation came to a head in Australia after a survey released earlier this month indicated sponsor recognition had been hijacked by companies not officially sponsoring the Games.

By example, the survey found 40 per cent of people incorrectly believed the national airline Qantas was an Olympic sponsor -- while less than 20 percent knew that rival airline Ansett was in fact an official Games partner.
Top international Olympic sponsors pay around US$40 million each over a four-year period for the right to use the Olympics to market their own brands.
Qantas has been running a series of ads featuring well known sports stars such as double Olympic swimming champion Kieren Perkins and Atlanta 400 metres silver medallist Cathy Freeman.
Palfreyman said while legislation was in place to stop non-sponsoring companies using intellectual property such as the Olympic rings, ambush marketing was not an illegal practice.
"What we're looking to do is develop a strategy to distinguish between just who and who isn't a real sponsor," Palfreyman said.
"We're not even suggesting that ambush marketing has taken place in Australia.

"We just want them (non-sponsors) to know that they should be careful about the way they go about their advertising campaigns so they don't give the impression to the man in the street that they have an an association with the Olympic Games."
Palfreyman added that SOCOG had spoken to several advertising agencies and expected a campaign to begin "as soon as possible".
A spokesman for Qantas dismissed SOCOG's move, saying Quantas had a long association in sponsoring Australian sport and athletes and would continue to do so.
At least 17 international aud Australian firms will provide sponsorship in cash and services for the 2000 Games.
The list of "Team Millennium Partners" includes traditional worldwide Olympic sponsors such as The Coca-Cola Co, International Business Machines Corp and Eastman Kodak Co.
National partners include Australian resources group The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp and Ansett Australia.
